name: Microsoft Hyper-V
summary: Microsoft’s type-1 hypervisor, built into Windows Server and Windows 10 and 11 Pro and Enterprise: a thin hypervisor under a Windows root partition, which also underpins Azure’s hypervisor and Windows features like VBS, WSL 2 and Windows Sandbox.
intro: Turning on Hyper-V slides the Microsoft hypervisor underneath Windows. The hypervisor’s main job is to create isolated partitions. The Windows install you started from becomes the root (or parent) partition: it runs the virtualization management stack and the device drivers, and it is the only partition with direct access to physical memory and devices. Each VM is a child partition, created through the hypercall API, that sees only virtual devices. Its requests travel over VMBus, a channel between partitions: a Virtualization Service Consumer (VSC) driver in the guest talks to a Virtualization Service Provider (VSP) in the root. These synthetic, “enlightened” devices for storage, networking, graphics and input skip hardware emulation, but the guest needs drivers that know about VMBus. Integration services provide them, plus heartbeat, shutdown, time sync and data exchange services; for Linux, these drivers (Linux Integration Services) are part of the kernel. Microsoft’s own 2009 slides call this a microkernel hypervisor with no device drivers, in contrast to monolithic hypervisors that carry their own driver model.

Generation 1 VMs emulate an older PC with BIOS, IDE disks and a legacy network card. Generation 2 VMs, added in Windows Server 2012 R2, use UEFI with Secure Boot on by default, boot from SCSI `.vhdx` disks up to 64 TB or over the network with the synthetic adapter, and drop the floppy and legacy devices. A VM’s generation can’t be changed after it is created. On Windows Server, live migration moves running VMs between hosts without perceived downtime, with or without shared storage, and Failover Clustering restarts a failed node’s VMs on another node. Hyper-V Replica keeps an asynchronous copy of a VM at another site, sending changes every 30 seconds, 5 minutes or 15 minutes. Nested virtualization runs Hyper-V inside a Hyper-V VM.

The same hypervisor sits under much of Windows and Azure. Virtualization-based security (VBS) uses it to create an isolated environment that hosts features like memory integrity. WSL 2 runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight utility VM. Windows Sandbox runs a separate, throwaway kernel. Windows containers started with `--isolation=hyperv` each run inside a highly optimized VM with their own kernel. Microsoft says “the Azure hypervisor system is based on Windows Hyper-V.” Hyper-V needs a 64-bit CPU with hardware virtualization and SLAT and isn’t available on Windows Home. Windows Server 2025 (November 2024, the current long-term release) supports up to 4 PB of memory and 2,048 logical processors per host, GPU partitioning and clusters outside Active Directory. The free standalone Hyper-V Server ended with the 2019 version: Microsoft said it would no longer offer the product, and its extended support ends in January 2029.
strengths: No separate hypervisor license: it ships with Windows Server and Windows Pro and Enterprise, and Windows Server Datacenter includes rights to unlimited Windows Server VMs

Drivers live in the Windows root partition, so it reuses Windows’ own hardware drivers, and it is managed with familiar tools: PowerShell, Hyper-V Manager, Windows Admin Center and System Center Virtual Machine Manager
Enterprise features in the box: live migration with or without shared storage, Failover Clustering, Hyper-V Replica with a 30-second interval, nested virtualization and GPU partitioning
Guests are well supported: Linux has its Hyper-V drivers upstream in the kernel, and generation 2 VMs boot with UEFI and Secure Boot
limits: No free standalone edition any more: Hyper-V Server 2019 was the last, with mainstream support ended in January 2024, so new hosts need a Windows Server or Windows Pro/Enterprise license

Everything runs through the root partition, a full Windows Server or Windows 10 or 11 Pro or Enterprise install that holds the management stack and every device driver (Windows Home can’t run Hyper-V)
Other hypervisors on the same PC suffer: Microsoft warns that VMware Workstation or VirtualBox VMs might not start or might run unreliably while the Hyper-V hypervisor is running
A VM’s generation is fixed at creation, and Linux distributions on older kernels may lack the latest Hyper-V driver fixes

sections.title: Generation 1 or generation 2?
sections.intro: From Microsoft’s guidance on choosing a VM generation. Microsoft recommends generation 2 unless the guest or the boot method needs generation 1.

rows.label: Firmware
values: UEFI, with Secure Boot on by default

rows.label: Boot disk
values: IDE controller: `.vhd`, `.iso` or a physical CD/DVD
Virtual SCSI: `.vhdx` up to 64 TB with online resize, or `.iso`

rows.label: Network boot
values: PXE through the legacy (emulated) network adapter
PXE over IPv4 and IPv6 through the synthetic adapter

rows.label: Other devices
values: Floppy and DMA controllers, UART for COM ports, i8042 keyboard controller
No floppy; optional UART for debugging; software-based input, with less emulation and a smaller attack surface

notes: A VM’s generation can’t be changed after it’s created. Since Windows Server 2025, Hyper-V Manager’s wizard picks generation 2 by default.

sections.title: Where Windows and Azure use the hypervisor
sections.intro: Hyper-V the role is the part you manage, but the same Microsoft hypervisor runs underneath these features.

items.name: Virtualization-based security
items.text: Uses hardware virtualization and the Windows hypervisor to create an isolated environment that assumes the kernel can be compromised, and hosts features such as memory integrity (HVCI) in it.

items.name: WSL 2
items.text: Runs a Linux kernel inside a lightweight utility VM; Linux distributions run as isolated containers inside that managed VM.

items.name: Windows Sandbox
items.text: A throwaway Windows desktop that relies on the Microsoft hypervisor to run a separate kernel, discarded when you close it.

items.name: Hyper-V isolated containers
items.text: Each Windows container runs in a highly optimized VM with its own kernel. It is the default for Windows containers on Windows 10 Pro and Enterprise.

items.name: Azure
items.text: Microsoft says the Azure hypervisor system is based on Windows Hyper-V, with a privileged root partition running the host OS and guest partitions for customer VMs.

story: Microsoft entered virtualization by buying Connectix’s virtual machine products, Virtual PC and Virtual Server, in February 2003. They were hosted products that ran on top of Windows. For servers Microsoft then built its own hypervisor: Hyper-V shipped with Windows Server 2008 and was released to manufacturing on June 26, 2008. Microsoft’s announcement called it “microkernelized” and contrasted it with “monolithic” solutions such as VMware ESX.

The design kept the hypervisor thin and reused Windows: drivers and the virtualization stack run in the root partition, so Hyper-V supported whatever hardware Windows supported. Later Windows Server releases filled in the data center features: live migration in Windows Server 2008 R2, Hyper-V Replica in Windows Server 2012 and generation 2 VMs with UEFI in Windows Server 2012 R2. The same hypervisor became the base of Azure’s hosts and, on the desktop, of features such as WSL 2, Windows Sandbox and virtualization-based security.

Microsoft also offered a free download, Hyper-V Server. It stopped after Hyper-V Server 2019, which Microsoft said was the last version of the free product. Hyper-V remains a role in Windows Server, and Windows Server 2025 raised its limits to 4 PB of memory and 2,048 logical processors per host.

choices.choice: A microkernel hypervisor with drivers in the root partition
choices.why: Microsoft’s architecture slides list the goals: a very thin, highly reliable hypervisor with no device drivers or third-party code, reusing the large base of existing Windows drivers instead.

choices.choice: Synthetic devices over VMBus instead of emulation
choices.why: Enlightened I/O for storage, networking, graphics and input bypasses device emulation, which is more efficient but needs guests with Hyper-V drivers, hence integration services and the Hyper-V drivers in the Linux kernel.
Hyper-V arrived as a role of Windows Server 2008, so anyone with Windows Server could run VMs without buying a separate hypervisor, and Datacenter licenses include unlimited Windows Server VMs.
Generation 2 dropped emulated legacy hardware for synthetic devices, UEFI and Secure Boot; generation 1 stayed for guests that still need BIOS and IDE.
